result:
Use the JSONL ledger.

The deciding factor is that humans read the records. JSONL is plain text: `less`, `grep`, `jq`, and a diff all work on it with no extra tooling. SQLite records need a client to inspect and produce no readable diff.

The volume settles the rest. About 5,000 lines a year stays well under a megabyte, so a full-file scan in Python or `jq` is instant and no index earns its keep. Single-threaded on one machine also removes SQLite's real advantage, concurrent-write safety via WAL, since there is no second writer. Append with `open(path, "a")` plus one `json.dumps` per line, and a crash mid-run costs you at most a trailing partial line.

Cost of the choice: no transactions across multiple records, no schema enforcement, and no indexed lookups. At this size those are cheap to live without. Add a `schema_version` field to each line so format changes stay readable later.

Reconsider if you gain concurrent writers, need queries that scan the whole history repeatedly, or pass roughly 100k records.
